POINT OF ORDER RESPECTING RULING ON SUB AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order concerning the subamendment which Your Honour accepted last night. I wish to make it perfectly clear that in doing so I am not in any way expressing opposition to, or discussing, the subject matter of the subamendment. In fact it was our party which in 1961 set up a royal commission to look into the whole question of medical services in Canada. The report of this commission is expected shortly.
My point is that Your Honour, after expressing grave doubts as to the acceptability of the subamendment last night, rendered a decision at 10.08 p.m. without waiting for hon. members to present their views as to the regularity and relevance of the subamendment. In this particular case I submit that Your Honour's ruling departs from established rulings on the principle of the relevancy of subamendments. With respect, it is the normal custom for Mr. Speaker to ask for the views of hon. members before making decisions on points of order such as the one that was before us last night. In the present case, Your Honour did indicate earlier your doubts as to the relevancy of the subamendment and seemed to indicate then that the subamendment was out of order. Subsequently, without any further discussion or opportunity for hon. members to present their views, Your Honour gave a contrary ruling. I and others of my colleagues were prepared to present certain views, and I know that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) had earlier expressed his intention of making his views known to the house.
Under the circumstances I would invite Your Honour, with respect, to reconsider your original decision and invite hon. members to present their views on the relevancy of the subamendment. In any event, may I point out respectfully that in such situations a ruling should not be made without calling for the views of hon. members present.

subtopic: POINT OF ORDER RESPECTING RULING ON SUB AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Last evening I gave my opinion that I had serious doubts about the relevancy of the subamendment. I think the authorities will show that good practice provides that subamendments should be relevant to the amendment. In the past, on the address a certain latitude has been given, not only in debate but in the wording of subamendments. I should like to give the house two examples. In 1952, when Speaker Ross Macdonald was in the Chair, Hon. Mr. Drew, seconded by Mr. Graydon, in amendment to the address moved:
We regret that Your Excellency's advisers
(a)	continue to impose excessive, burdensome and unjust taxation;
(b)	refuse to eliminate waste and extravagance and to cut down the cost of government;
(c)	fail to take adequate steps to deal effectively with inflation and the high cost of living.
Then Mr. Coldwell, seconded by Mr. Knowles, moved in amendment to the proposed amendment the following:
This house further regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to recommend the inauguration of a national health insurance program, with provision for provincial participation.

subtopic: POINT OF ORDER RESPECTING RULING ON SUB AMENDMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: POINT OF ORDER RESPECTING RULING ON SUB AMENDMENT

Nevertheless the house accepted them at the time for debate, although they were rejected subsequently.
Last night, when no one rose to object I decided to accept the subamendment, even though I had doubts about its relevancy. In accepting this subamendment I endeavoured to suggest to the house that in future subamendments should be relevant in spite of considerable latitude given in the past. I will comply with the rules of the house and answer the questions just asked by the right hon. gentleman. He asked what steps had been taken. I informed the house on Wednesday that a special commission had been established to consider all matters relating to the security of national defence property. The commission had begun its investigation on January 31 and made its report yesterday. The recommendations include a number of long term measures which are now being studied by the chiefs of staff.
One recommendation relates to immediate action. It is that all serviceable small arms and ammunition be withdrawn from reserve establishments where maximum security cannot be provided. Consequent upon that recommendation, an order has gone out today that all small arms be withdrawn from reserve establishments where maximum security cannot be provided on an around the clock basis. In addition, orders have gone out today that at least one person will be on duty at reserve establishments on an around the clock basis. This procedure will be implemented just as quickly as it is feasible to do so. The longer term measures which have been recommended are being studied and will be implemented just as expeditiously as it is felt advisable to do so.
In respect of law enforcement, we have to be very careful not to interfere with the jurisdiction of local police forces who have, under our constitution, the responsibility in these matters. However, we are co-operating in every respect, fully and completely, with them in the performance of their duties, to

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: USE OF MAILS FOR DISSEMINATION OF RACIAL DISCRIMINATION LITERATURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Postmaster General. Are the postal authorities contemplating any action against the national white Americans party, who are using the Canadian mails to disseminate literature encouraging racial discrimination and advocating, among other things, the sterilization of people of the Jewish race?

maintopic: USE OF MAILS FOR DISSEMINATION OF RACIAL DISCRIMINATION LITERATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that this is a matter of some urgency, and I might say my attention was drawn to it a few hours ago. There is no question but that this organization has been using the mails just within the last day or so to promote racial prejudice in an organized way. It is not a case of a crank. It is the work of an organization, but while the thing is disturbing and shocking I personally do not think the Post Office Department has been or should be set up to act as a censor, certainly not in peacetime. However, in view of the seriousness of the matter I have discussed it with my colleague the Minister of Justice and officials of my own department.
If the hon. member and other hon. members of the house have received letters of this nature from their constituents or others I would appreciate it if they would forward them to me, and particularly the envelopes or containers if they have them, so that I can follow it up with the officials of the Department of Justice and with the provincial authorities.

Mr. Speaker, while I am on my feet I would like to give a full answer to the question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek which I took as notice. The question was:
In view of the fact that this government has changed its policy with regard to community pastures without informing the house, would the minister now disclose the terms of his new policy to members of parliament?
These are the major changes:
1.	Grazing fees were increased from 3J cents per day per head to 5 cents, with an additional 1 cent per day to reimburse municipalities for the loss of tax revenue.
2.	P.F.R.A. assumes responsibility for allocation of grazing privileges based on individual need, proximity to the pasture and its past uses.
3.	The advisory committee will have six members and no member will hold office for more than two consecutive terms.
4.	A general meeting of pasture patrons will be held every two years. Special meetings may be called if necessary.
5.	Each patron will be required to remit a deposit of $2 per head for cattle accepted for grazing. This will help to eliminate the difficulty due to padded allocations and subsequent non-delivery of cattle.
6.	Preference for allocation will be given to breeding stock in view of the increase in cow-calf enterprise.

The house resumed, from Thursday, February 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. FEBRUARY 21, 1984
Jean-Pierre Cote (Longueuil) for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Douglas.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset, may I heartfully congratulate the mover (Mr. Cote, Longueuil) and the seconder (Mr. Basford) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
But as can be seen on page 23 of Hansard for February 19, the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard discussed a matter which I shall deal with briefly later on.
But the mover and seconder had an unpleasant task, that is to bring forward in a decent dressing the menu for this session which unfortunately contains nothing very tempting, nothing very delicious for the Canadian people.
They discharged their duty very well and their oratory made us forget how empty was the speech from the throne and how it is more particularly remarkable by what it suggests and leaves unsaid.
May I say here that despite their eloquent speeches the mover and seconder did not succeed in convincing the members of our group, nor the Canadian people at large.
Mr. Speaker, at this stage of my remarks, 1 also wish to congratulate the new ministers, including the Minister without Portfolio who, according to some reports, obtained that position because of his fight against Social credit in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, like the previous government, this Liberal government seems to be characterized by arrogance, irresolution and the lack of leadership needed for the sound administration of state business.
The speech from the throne indicates that our statesmen have travelled. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) went to Paris and Washington.
What was the result of their representations to General de Gaulle? Right from the start, the press represented the Prime Minister as a middleman, or emissary, who would eliminate any source of friction between Paris and Washington. Yet, they soon had to sing a different tune, because, after the Prime Minister's visit to Washington, Canada announced its intention to withdraw its squadrons stationed at Grostenquin, in France, and to station them in Germany, because General de Gaulle did not want any foreign aircraft with nuclear equipment on French
The Address-Mr. Caouette soil. That is one result of the Liberal government's nuclear policy and of the Prime Minister's visit to Paris.
And there is another result. The Prime Minister was apparently told by General de Gaulle himself that France would recognize communist China. However, nothing has been said about the Canadian Prime Minister's reaction. We had hoped that the Prime Minister would throw some light on the attitude the Canadian government means to take with regard to such a serious and controversial matter.
I am now coming to the problem of Cyprus where two members of NATO are in opposite camps, that is, Turkey and Greece. Some big financial interests are also implicated. At the first news of the conflict, the press announced that Canada was ready to send a force of one thousand men to preserve peace in Cyprus. What we do not understand, we who belong to the Ralliement Creditistes, is that the Liberal government acts so hurriedly in external affairs matters and problems which only affect us in a remote way, whereas this same government is so undecided and inactive when it comes to deal with problems concerning all Canadians.
On February 14, I sent to the Prime Minister of Canada a telegram that read as follows:
Hon. Lester B. Pearson, Prime Minister of Canada
House of Commons
Ottawa.
Re: Conflict between Greeks and Turks in Cyprus stop We have no commitment toward Cyprus stop Please do not interefere, nor commit yourself, nor send troops to Cyprus without consulting Canadian parliament stop Members meeting next week will decide policy.
Liberals and Conservatives alike are always anxious to interfere, to mobilize armed forces for risky ventures in all corners of the world. Such attitude is not new. It dates back from Laurier, who sent to the rescue of the British some Canadian troops against the Boers in Transvaal. It went on under Borden who during the first world war, set his police and his packs of dogs at the French Canadians' heels when all they asked was to live in peace.
This went on with King and St. Laurent who mobilized all human, industrial and financial resources in Canada to fight the war against the axis powers.
When it comes to waging war, there is no indecision but quick and positive action; men and arms are available and money is forthcoming to meet the cost.
For instance, Mr. Speaker, nobody would say that there is no money to send Canadian troops to Cyprus, but it is claimed that there is no money to help the unemployed, to provide them with a decent standard of living

The Address-Mr. Caouette and to increase family allowances. In Cyprus, our troops would be well dressed, well housed, well fed, but in Canada the unemployed are compelled by the Liberal government to take a shovel and dig in frozen ground under the winter works program while power shovels and bulldozers stand idle in heated garages, close to the places which these labourers are working in bitter cold.
Such is the logic of the system and of the government provided by the Liberals.
This morning, I received from Arvida, in the Jonquiere constituency, a picture which appeared in Le Lingot of Arvida, on February 13, 1964; here is what we read:
This picture shows some 20 men trying to remove a small mound in a field where the St. Michel road might pass some day, in order to cut out a curve. So as to ensure work for the greater number, they use shovels, picks and wheelbarrows.
Why not use teaspoons, in order to give work to the 400,000 unemployed in Canada?
What a brilliant system.
The people of Canada do not want our government and our troops to intervene in Cyprus where they have no business.
On February 18, I received the following telegram from the Greek community of metropolitan Toronto:
Three thousand Canadians of Greek origin, gathered at the Kingsway Club and representing the 45,000 residents of the district, request your support concerning the territorial integrity of Cyprus and the right of the Cypriots to constitute a peaceful nation free from any intimidation or intervention on the part of other countries.
(Signed) E. Ghikadis, Chairman,
P. Economides, Secretary, The Greek Community of metropolitan Toronto.
Yesterday, I received another telegram from Vancouver which I will read in English.

As Canadian citizens of Hellenic ancestry the Hellenes in this area through the Hellenic community of Vancouver respectfully appeal to you to support the rights of the * Cypriots to survive as a nation and to live in peace as free men within a democratic national of Cyprus.

That is the telegram I received from Vancouver yesterday.
Mr. Speaker, Canadian affairs must be the foremost concern of members of the house and of parliament itself. Let us look after our own business and matters of interest to the Canadian people.
What did the government give the Canadian people during the last session?
It gave them gifts that they had no use for.

First gift: nuclear weapons, built to spread destruction and death, in order not to meet the needs and the wishes of Canadians, but rather to please our American neighbours and to serve as an advanced line of defence for the United States. That was a Christmas present from the Liberal government to the Canadian people.
A second gift: the increase in the old age security tax to pay $10 a month more to the old people of Canada. If the old age security tax has to be raised by 1 per cent to provide for a $10 per month increase in the pension, what is going to be the cost of the famous portable pension scheme mentioned in the speech from the throne?
A third gift: the 11 per cent tax on building materials, which amounts to a penalty imposed upon building contractors and construction workers as well as home buyers.
On that subject, here is a statement made by the Canadian Labour Congress, an organization representing over one million workers, in the February 1964 issue of Canadian Labour.
In December, the unemployed made up 5.1 per cent of the whole labour force, that is 346,000 Canadian workers. Among them, 73,000 or more than one out of five workers, had been without work for at least four months and more than one out of ten had been unemployed for seven months or more. Their pride hurt, their skills impaired and their faith in the future lessened through a prolonged period of unemployment, many of these workers are already beyond help or close to it.
Another serious aspect of the present unemployment crisis is the fact that a great many of our young men become unemployed as soon as they leave school. The most recent data show, indeed, that 10 per cent of the workers between 14 and 19 are without work, which is twice the average for all age groups.
Drives to encourage students to finish high school or technical training courses and the implementation of vocational training programs will contribute, of course, the solution of the problem, but those efforts will not give a job to those who are already unemployed or to the post-war generation which is beginning to come on the labour market.
To solve the unemployment problem in an affluent society, it is not enough to adopt scattered measures. What is the use, for instance, of granting a $500 bonus on a house built during the winter months when, on the other hand, its price goes up by $800 on account of the tax on building materials?
Nobody can argue that building a house in the winter costs the same as in the spring, summer or fall. The working conditions are not the same and any carpenter who knows how to handle a hammer will tell you that under a temperature of 40 below zero, it cannot be handled the same way as during spring, summer or autumn.
The Canadian Labour Congress suggested far-reaching means for curing this evil.
Hence, even though we can rejoice that recently fewer Canadians were seeking jobs, we must not regard the unemployed as mere statistics. How can we be satisfied that only 5.1 per cent of the

labour force is unemployed? This figure, quite low in appearance, represents hundreds of thousands of Canadians seeking desperately a means of earning a living for themselves and their families, of taking part in the advancement of Canada.
Another gift from the Liberals to the Canadian people is the salary raise for members of parliament; their salary increased from $10,000 to $18,000, while the pension of our senior citizens increased by only $10 a month, to a total of $75 a month.
Following those new taxes and big salary raises for members of parliament, senators, judges and government officials, the Canadian people expected their government to bring in at the very beginning of this session measures likely to raise the standard of living of all Canadian families, and which would have received, I am sure, the unanimous support of all parties in this house.
But there was no such thing. On the contrary, the principal legislative measures announced in the speech from the throne relate to controversial matters which will create division rather than unity.
To mention only one case, I will refer to the grant of loans to students which has been announced in the speech from the throne. One of the chief measures advocated in the speech from the throne deals with interest-free loans which could be secured by university students.
This is a commendable step: to help students to complete their studies and finish their education. It undoubtedly fills a need since a great majority of students have to live in want, to impose hardships on their parents who sometimes become destitute to enable their children to continue their studies.
But we do not believe that the federal proposal is the appropriate measure. In the first place, it constitutes an encroachment on the rights reserved to the provinces, which must remain masters of their educational system. The solution, in this case, is to return to the provinces the taxation authority which is theirs, and to provide the funds necessary for social and cultural development through the Bank of Canada, if need be.
Besides, the system of loans made by the federal government is bound to increase the risks of patronage, of electoral blackmailing of students who will have to get loans through intermediaries.
The speech from the throne also mentions that we shall be called upon to approve the changes in fiscal arrangements with the provinces, decided upon at the federal-provincial conference last November.
There is no need to recall Premier Lesage's famous ultimatum of April 5, 1963, formulated in the following words to the Quebec legislature:
20220-7i
The Address-Mr. Caouette
I solemnly state that I cannot continue indefinitely to talk about the needs of the province of Quebec or to be satisfied to submit requests to the central government in the hope that it will condescend to meet them. As I said a moment ago, this subject is of the utmost importance and I do not intend as premier and minister of finance to repeat these things year after year without obtaining any tangible results. Hence, it is the last time that I reiterate them in such terms in the budget speech.
Twelve months will go by before the next budget speech. Either the central government, regardless of the party that will come into power on April 8-I repeat, regardless of the party that will come into power on April 8-will have availed itself of the 12-month period to take into consideration the requirements of the province of Quebec or we, from Quebec, will have for our part and during the said period decided upon the measures required in matters of taxation. And those decisions will be dictated to us by the economic, social and cultural self-assertion which we set up as our objective, according to the wishes of the people of Quebec.
"25-25-100"; those three figures had practically become a slogan in Quebec, where in most cases the man in the street did not even know that they represented the minimum percentage of revenue claimed by the Lesage government with regard to personal and corporation income taxes and succession duties.
Now, last November, Premier Lesage suggested an amendment of the present fiscal arrangements and claimed from the federal government a per capita yield of $77.03 instead of $49.74 per capita which Quebec is getting at present. Quebec would therefore have received $420 million instead of $272 million.
That was, on the part of Quebec, another concession to the promoters of federal centralization. Indeed, what Quebec wants most, is not 10, 15, 25, or even 50 per cent of its taxation rights, but 100 per cent. Quebec wants to be able to develop within confederation, according to its aspirations and needs. To that end, it needs all its sources of revenue, without prejudice to anybody's rights or privileges, whether he be from Alberta, Ontario, Saskatchewan or any other province of this country.
Now, Mr. Lesage only obtained $42,716,000 of the $148 million he was claiming as his minimum needs.
We, members of the Social Credit rally, who represent the legitimate interests of this nation, shall not be a party to Quebec's enslavement by the central authority. We shall always claim that all its lawful rights be returned to the province of Quebec.
As concerns the portable pension plan, referred to by the government in the speech from the throne, we admit that it is necessary to seek a formula allowing the workers who change jobs to keep the benefits accrued in a pension fund to which they have

The Address-Mr. Caouette contributed. But, again, we do not believe the fair and equitable formula is that of a state fund administered by the state. We are opposed to the very principle of these state pension funds, whether they are administered by the federal or provincial governments. We believe that the state is not supposed to administer everything, to control everything, to direct everything, but to act as a substitute.
Briefly, here are the main reasons why we oppose the federal plan and that of the province of Quebec.
Those federal or provincial pension funds, if they are intended to create huge capital to which governments will resort to undertake various works, will have the following consequences.
First, they will forcibly drain the savings of the people into the hands of the government, so that private enterprise will be short of money and capital to develop and expand. Private enterprise will have to resort to bank borrowing or sale of shares and bonds in foreign countries to obtain the money needed.
Second, they will place in the hands of the state such a power that it will be able to control all economic activities of the country, or of a country, in this instance, our own.
Third, they will discourage free and voluntary savings among the people by the establishment of compulsory and forced savings plans.
Fourth, the amounts loaned with interest by the pension funds will some day have to be paid back by means of taxes. Those taxes will be paid by Canadian taxpayers who, after having been forced to put their savings in the fund, will have to pay back those savings thus loaned, as well as the interest, doubling in 20 years the amount loaned, so that the taxpayers will have paid twice their pension plan.
In this connection, the attitude of the Ralliement Creditistes is as follows: The Ralliement Creditistes is of the opinion that the Bank of Canada Act should be amended this very year, because it is in 1964, that the banks' charters and the federal banking legislation will have to be renewed. It seems to me that it is high time to amend the Bank of Canada Act so that it may credit the Canadian government with the amounts of money that might be necessary from time to time to increase purchasing power and the money supply of the country. This new purchasing power could be distributed in several ways; social security benefits, public debt redemption, financing of social equipment, price reductions to the consumers and finally dividend payments to everybody.
One of the major tasks and one of the


first tasks of a Creditiste government would be to obtain an amount sufficient to provide everybody with the standard of living permitted by the resources of the country.
On the other hand, if those benefits or annuities came from new money created by the Bank of Canada, it would result in income tax cuts, for the government would not have to take away from the taxpayers, for its own purpose, hundreds of millions of dollars, and this would help to raise everybody's purchasing power. This is what is being done in the United States, where the President announced income tax cuts of $11 and $22 billion to provide the American people with increased purchasing power and to promote a sound American economy. If tax cuts are good and auspicious for the United States, if they are logical at this time, why would they not be the same here in Canada, when our economy is almost paralysed by an obsolete monetary system not adjusted to real physical possibilities and to the needs of our people?
Finally, the speech from the throne talks about strengthening and developing primary and secondary industry in Canada to provide employment.
Is the major problem in Canada today to provide employment? Is that really what Canada needs, to set up new industries while the existing ones have slowed down their production because it cannot be marketed?
As far as we are concerned, we think that industry in all its aspects does not have the responsibility to provide employment, but rather to provide products and services.
Our industrial organization will be all the more perfect if it can produce with less human labour, leaving man free to exercise his faculties at carrying out humanizing and liberating activities.
The main reason why it is so difficult to find a solution to today's problems is that everybody, politicians, press, governments and labour movements seem to think that the objective of economic activities is to provide employment.
I should like to quote here Rev. Georges-Henri Levesque, O.P., who wrote in 1937, that is 25 or 30 years ago:
The nature of things, sound reason and social justice tell us that the purpose of economic activities can be nothing but the material prosperity of society, the welfare of the whole human community.
The economy should be designed, not to create wealth for itself or a happy few, but to meet the needs of all and produce goods which would be of real benefit to every citizen of this country. In the language of economics, it would be even more accurate to say: The aim is to serve the consumer, every consumer. The consumer comes first. That should be the main slogan of any policy truly social and humanitarian.

What is needed before anything else is purchasing power for Canadian families, if economic recovery is to be achieved in Canada while everybody, every politician, every newspaper, is shouting: "Beware of unemployment, beware of the unemployed; jobs for all, jobs for all." The more talk there is about full employment, the greater the number of unemployed in Canada. Industries are shutting down because their products no longer sell.
That is why any government, whether it be Liberal, Conservative, Social Credit or N.D.P., must look to the Canadian consumers so that they may set and maintain the economic power in Canada.
This will materialize only when a greater purchasing power is available to the Canadian people, allowing them to purchase the goods which our Canadian industry can produce thanks to the machines and the technological developments.
It is the Canadian families' purchasing power which must be increased first, not through taxes taken out of the workers' pay envelopes, which results in a lower purchasing power, but by paying them new money, so as to restore the balance with new money, not as the new minister of useless affairs, the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Na-pierville (Mr. Dupuis) likes to say, by printing money without consideration-but by giving them new money in order to balance the country's real credit with the financial credit.
Real credit is the true assessment of the capability of producing and delivering goods and services in sufficient quantity at the right time and place to suit the consumers.
Real credit rests on goods, material things. Real credit is the wealth of a country, a province, in possible goods and services.
Financial credit is the assessment of the capability of delivering money in sufficient quantity at the right time and place.
Real credit is based on tangible things or certainties and originates in some manner in the goodness of the Creator who put in the ground, in the water and in the air all the required wealth for the satisfaction of men, to whom He gave intelligence, brains and hands to use those resources; as for financial credit, which should reflect actual credit, it is an invention of men, a thing invented by individuals and organizations or banks, which can control it and make it scarce whenever they please.
Where is the solution? In the balance of financial and actual credit as advocated by Social Crediters.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to extend my own congratulations to the two new members for Laurier (Mr. Leblanc) and St. Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) though I deplore the fact that only 32 per cent of the voters troubled to cast their vote.
Whether this regret is expressed by myself or by anyone in the house, I believe that if we want to save democracy, it will be necessary to establish a political climate which will' cause the electors to go and cast their votes.
Sixty five per cent of the electors in these two electoral districts did not cast their votes. How can the hon. member conclude that the

The Address-Mr. Caouette people approve the Liberal government policy, and state that the Creditistes are losing ground in the province of Quebec, when a recent Gallup poll published in the Western Producer mentioned that, in the province of Quebec, the Creditistes were regaining ground?
The following are a few remarks made, not by a Creditiste but by an independent newspaperman, Maurice Huot, of Le Droit. Everyone knows this journalist for his cool and logical analysis of such matters. This is what he had to say the day after the elections:
The two by-elections showed that if the two old parties took the lion's share in a riding like that of St. Denis, the Ralliement Creditistes was a source of annoyance for them and that in Laurier, it was a real threat since it took the second place away from the Conservatives by several hundred votes.
In view of the fact that, in Laurier, the candidate of the Ralliement Creditistes got the same proportion of votes as in 1963, in spite of the division of Social Credit into two branches in the House of Commons and the determined fight carried on against it by the Liberal party in the last general election, the latter will certainly want to reconsider the situation. Prudence will perhaps dictate that the best course of action for the present time is to keep quiet.
Here are the official statistics for the last three elections, in 1962, 1963 and 1964, in the constituencies of Laurier and St. Denis.
Out of 26,000 voters in Laurier, 16,773 voted in 1962, 18,226 in 1963, and 10,348 in 1964.

Mr. Speaker, the riding of St. James where I had the privilege and honour to be elected to the federal parliament, is a county which has existed since confederation and in which lives an industrious and almost exclusively French-speaking population. The remaining population consists of a number of Canadians of various origins with whom we fraternize and pursue the achievement of a Canadian nation.
The county of St. James runs along the bank of the St. Lawrence river and contains part of the old Montreal, to which so much Canadian history is attached by so many bonds. Arrangements have been made to preserve the original character of that city

district. Municipal authorities, the Jacques Viger commission, and the historical sites commission took concerted action to establish the south central sector of the city as an historical district. As a Canadian citizen, Mr. Speaker, who learned as a child to speak and to respect the English language, I am most happy to express myself in a language which is the language of my fellow citizens and the vast majority of the North American population as well as several countries throughout the world.

Canada is an adult nation, called upon to play a prominent part in the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic party welcomes most heartily the good things that are contained in the speech from the throne. There are a few good items in it, and we shall do our best to see to it that these good items are enacted into legislation at the earliest possible date.
The New Democratic party also regrets very strongly the serious omissions from the speech from the throne, and we shall do our best during the course of this session to persuade the government to make up for these omissions by bringing in some of the items which ought to have been included. Reference has been made already to a number of these items, but may I list them briefly so that the government may know what to expect from us by way of demands during the course of this session.
We believe this government should be bringing in provision for a federal-provincial medicare program, and we shall be asking the house to vote on this at a quarter to six this afternoon. We also regret that the Canadian development corporation, which was proposed in the speech from the throne last year, has been omitted. There was also the omission of any reference to improving the Unemployment Insurance Act. There is the omission of university scholarships, which in our view has not been taken care of by loans to students. There is also the omission of any proposal for improving the Family Allowances Act.
Likewise, despite the apparent conversion at the last session of this house to the principle of economic planning suggested in the speeches on the bill which set up the Department of Industry and the bill setting up the Economic Council of Canada, there is nothing in the present speech from the throne to indicate that the government realizes that in this day and age economic planning is a necessity if we are to achieve the kind of economy which will provide full employment and security for all our people. We shall, in the course of this session, do our best to get the government to bring in some of these things it forgot to put in the speech from the throne.
I may say, also, that we in this party welcome the type of speech which the Prime Minister made in this debate. I think it would be agreed on all sides of the house that it was a tremendous improvement over the speech the same right hon. gentleman made in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne last session, and even more of an improvement over the one that he made two sessions ago. He refrained from being baited by the Leader of the Opposition,

and chose rather to tell us what the government of which he is now the head proposes to do.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, we welcome this type of speech from the leader of the government. But having made the kind of speech that he did last evening, he perhaps should be given a word of warning. It seemed to me that he was endeavouring to cast himself in the role of a social and political reformer. He used the words "social and political reform" on two or three occasions. He referred to the pieces of legislation that the government proposes to proceed with as examples of social and political reform. This is fine, Mr. Speaker, provided that the same Prime Minister and the government of which he is the head deliver the goods.
I am sure that, as the leader of the Liberal party, he will not be surprised that some of us do not clap our hands for joy when the Liberal party announces itself as the party of reform, because after all that is the stance the Liberal party in this country has taken throughout the lifetime of all of us who are in this chamber, whatever our age. For far too long this stance has been one that has deceived the Canadian people. Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King was a past master at appearing as a protagonist of reform, getting elected on this basis and taking years and years, decades and decades, to put on the statute books some of the things that were promulgated in the name of reform. So if the present Prime Minister wishes to take this stance, if he wishes to appear as an apostle of reform, well and good; but I suggest that he deliver the goods, otherwise the Canadian people will not take kindly to the idea of again being fooled by the Liberal party that has done it to the Canadian people so often.
That leads me to the main body of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, during which I shall deal with three of the subjects that the Prime Minister himself touched upon last evening. Other subjects that he spoke of will be dealt with by colleagues of mine during the course of this debate but, as I say, I shall confine myself to three of the subjects that he dealt with as being in the eyes of the government, in the eyes of all of us, very important.
The first of these subjects is the Canada pension plan. I was delighted to hear the Prime Minister say last night that he regards this as one of the most important pieces of legislation to be enacted at this session. We were told in the speech from the throne that it would be laid before us. We were told, in response to a question I put to the Prime Minister the other day, that it would be given high priority and proceeded with in the early days of this session. We were told the same
The Address-Mr. Knowles thing last night by the Prime Minister in his speech; that it has priority, that it will be proceeded with.
These are wonderful words to hear, Mr. Speaker, but I hope I do not sound cynical if I remind the government that we heard precisely the same words at the last session. We came to this house at the last session fresh from an election campaign in which the Canada pension plan was promised by the Liberal party. It was the keystone in the arch of the victory they won last April. It was promised in the speech from the throne. It was promised in answers to questions on orders of the day. In the speech the Prime Minister made in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne last May he confirmed that it would be enacted at that session. But everyone knows that because of opposition that arose, all we had was one day's debate on the resolution preceding the bill, and that was as far as we got.
Now we have the revision of the plan. As my leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), pointed out last night, we have the third version of the Canada pension plan as presented to us by the Liberals, and it is watered down to an extent that we deplore. I want to say to the Prime Minister that though by common consent he made an excellent speech last night, there were two or three very weak points in it. I thought one of the weakest was when he tried to explain that reducing the benefits to be obtained under the Canada pension plan was not really a reduction because under the plan of last July the ratio of benefits was to be 30 per cent at age 70 and 20 per cent at age 65, and under the new plan it is still 20 per cent at age 65, even though it is no higher at age 70. So somehow or other we are supposed to believe that the benefits have not actually been reduced. The benefits at age 65 under last year's plan, were a reduction of the normal benefits to be available at age 70, and we are now being given a plan which will cost the people of Canada more, but the benefits will be less.
We suggest that this is a retreat; that it is hardly the proper performance for a party that takes the position of being a party of social reform. I think attention should be paid to the demand my leader made last night, that the plan be restored to what it was last July, and that this parliament be given an opportunity to enact it in that form at this session.
This is not the first time we have been in the position of seeing progressive legislation stalled because of lobbies against it. I can think of many other instances during the years I have been here. I will not take the time to mention them, but I am very much

The Address-Mr. Knowles aware of what happened last year and we are all very much aware of the position that still exists, of the position being taken by Mr. Robarts and the communications still being sent out by Mr. Kilgour, the president of the Great-West Life Assurance Company of my own city; and we cannot help but be concerned that these pressures will again have the effect of dissuading the government from keeping its promise and going ahead with the plan this session. The promise has been made that the legislation will be referred to committee which means, of course, after second reading.

Lesage is not forgotten in this house; he is mentioned many times, almost every day. The bill will be referred to committee after second reading, no doubt. I hope that this reference to a committee which the government has promised, because it has been asked to do so by those in favour of the plan as well as by those against it, will not be used as an excuse for such a long delay that the bill will not get through. That can happen. In committee all kinds of bodies and organizations can appear, debate can go on and on, and before we know it, it could be too late in the session to put the measure through. I suggest that the house make up its mind. The people of Canada voted for something like this on April 8, 1963, and it is our responsibility to see that this legislation gets through at this session without fail.
The second of the subjects with which the Prime Minister dealt last night concerning which I should like to say a few words is the question of a national labour code. It was on November 8 of last year, during the first session of this parliament, that the Minister of Labour, in response to questions during the discussion of his estimates, gave a virtual promise that at this session of parliament a national labour code would be brought in by the government. We are glad, therefore, to see the assurance in the speech from the throne that this will be done. We are glad also that the Prime Minister confirmed in the speech he made last night that this legislation will be introduced and will be given high priority at this session.
Again, as my leader pointed out last night, you can hardly expect us to jump for joy over this sign of progress on the part of the Liberal party. I have here two interesting books which are to be found in the library of this parliament. They both go back to 1919. This larger one contains all the resolutions and proposals which were submitted to the Liberal national convention of 1919 held here in the city of Ottawa, and it makes very interesting reading. If one goes through this


volume he will find that a major section of the resolutions presented concerned labour relations, on the basis of which the Liberal party wanted to take a stand for a minimum wage, for a maximum work day, for a maximum work week, for vacations, and for standards which would protect workers so far as health and safety were concerned.
That is the one book. The other book is a report of the Liberal convention in 1919, and it contains the consolidated resolutions which were passed. The Liberal party almost 45 years ago took a stand for progress in this field, a stand for a national labour code, a minimum wage law, a maximum work day, a maximum work week, and the other matters. It is hardly an indication of speed that it has taken 45 years for a Liberal government to bring in a piece of legislation of this kind. Incidentally, it was given to the then Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King to make his main speech at that convention, apart from the one which he made at the end after he had been elected leader, on the question of labour relations. He gave a stirring pledge as to what the Liberal party would do to make things better for the working people of Canada by enacting into legislation these things which that party promised way back in 1919.
As I say, you can hardly expect us to jump for joy, but we are at least glad that at long last we are seeing these things appearing before us in legislative form. I suggest that before the bill is presented to us, whether it is preceded by a resolution or comes in directly as a bill, the government give very serious consideration to its terms. Let it be not a weak bill hardly worthy of being passed. Let it propose standards which are worth while in this day and age.
The suggestion is that there will be in the national labour code a minimum wage. I suggest it be not less than $1.25 an hour. Indeed, by now that figure should be higher, but it should certainly be not less than $1.25 an hour. Let there be no distinction as between men and women. Let there be no distinctions among various areas of the country. Let that minimum wage apply to all workers who come under federal labour jurisdiction.
In the matter of maximum working hours or a maximum working week, let it be not less than a five day, 40 hour week. I suggest there be included a provision similar to that contained in the bill on the order paper in the name of my colleague the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott), which would make it possible for those hours to be reduced as technological improvements and automation make it necessary for us to have a shorter

working week. Let the provision for statutory holidays include at least eight or nine of them.
Let the bill also include something about vacations with pay. Nothing was said in the speech from the throne or in the speech yesterday of the Prime Minister on this point. I realize we have a Vacations With Pay Act on the statute books, but it has at least two main weaknesses. One is that it takes two years before the two weeks which are allotted become effective; the other is that there is no provision for escalating that two week vacation into anything more no matter how long an employee works for a corporation which comes under federal labour jurisdiction. Hon. members know of my bills on the order paper, one of which calls for two weeks vacation with pay after one year and the other for three weeks after five years. I suggest that provisions which are at least as good as these ought to be included in this legislation.
Then there is the question of providing health and safety standards. Let these things be well thought out and let them appear in the bill, so that some of the provisions to protect the position of workers in industry, and the workers of the country generally, which Mackenzie King proclaimed 45 years ago, will at last become part of the law of this land. I would remind Liberal members of the house that Mr. King was very specific when he made his speech at the conclusion of that convention for he stated that his was the party which would take these resolutions which they had passed at their convention and enact them into legislation and make them the law of the land. Let us do that at long last, at this session.
I also plead with the government of the day to pay no attention to some of the voices which are being raised in connection with the enactment of a national labour code. In particular I suggest that the government pay no attention to that great Liberal journal, the Winnipeg Free Press. It agrees with the idea of a national labour code, but it wants it to include not only minimum standards to protect workers but as well certain restrictive provisions to hold in check the strength and bargaining power of the trade union movement.
I suggest that is entirely a different subject. That sort of thing is covered, if it needs to be covered, by the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. I suggest rather that the national labour code should be a charter for labour. There is nothing in the speech from the throne to suggest that any of this other kind of legislation will be included; but I know the kind of pressure which will be exerted, and I urge the govern-
The Address-Mr. Knowles ment to stick to the kinds of things that it has said, through the mouth of the Minister of Labour and through the speech from the throne, are to be included in this legislation.
This is a subject, Mr. Speaker, concerning which many proposals have been made in the House of Commons. My bills and the bills of some of my colleagues have been on the order paper for a long time. Resolutions have been introduced and speeches have been made. But apart from the equal pay for equal work legislation which the previous Liberal administration brought in and the Vacations With Pay Act that the last Conservative administration brought in, there has not been introduced in the House of Commons from the government side of the house at any time a comprehensive national labour code. I hope this is not a case of it having to be done two, three or half a dozen times, as is the case with some legislation. That is the way the first old age pension legislation started out in 1926 and 1927, and that is the way it is at this time with the Canada pension plan and the Canada development corporation. Let us face the fact that the thinking on this subject is well jelled; let us recognize that this is a good piece of legislation, and, let us see to it that we get it through at this session of parliament.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that there were three matters to which I wished to devote my time this afternoon, and the third matter is the question of parliament itself. I think it was a good sign that both the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister had something to say in their remarks yesterday about this institution of parliament. I believe they reflect the views of all of us in drawing attention to parliament. I believe they reflect the desire of all of us to improve the job which we are doing in this place on behalf of the people of Canada. We earnestly desire this institution to be the glorious one that historically it is reputed to be; and that it do the best job it can in terms of the needs of this day and age.
However, Mr. Speaker, I could not help but notice yesterday, despite the worthy statements made by both these right hon. gentlemen on the subject of parliament, that when it came to specific examples each of them saw something wrong on the other side. When the Leader of the Opposition had something to talk about in terms of what is wrong with parliament, what was it? It was the way in which the Liberal government acts. His example, of course, was that the Liberal government in the last session transferred too many notices of motions for production of papers to the item

The Address-Mr. Knowles under which they can be debated and then talked them out. This was pretty had, he said, and I agree it was bad. It was also bad the session before, when from the Liberal side of the house there was the motion for the production of papers with regard to the surcharge order. The Conservative government of that day transferred that motion to the item under which it could be debated, and then talked that out for the session.
However, that is just by the way. The point I am making is that the principal example which the Leader of the Opposition advanced to show something was wrong was something which he saw over on the other side of the house.
The Prime Minister, in effect, did the same thing. He had some suggestions to make. Time must be saved. The suggestions he made were at the expense of the opposition. Parliament must be improved. We must streamline our procedures, and we must expedite the business of the house. But how was this to be done? It was to be done by the opposition talking less in order to get the business through. I suppose it is human nature and it is typical that when anything is wrong in any group or society it is the other fellow who should make the corrections. I suggest that if we are going to improve parliament, and I think we all agree that we should, we are going to have to admit that there are faults on both sides. There is room for improvement on both sides. We have to look at the problem in its totality rather than finding ways of blaming the other fellow.
As a matter of fact, if time permits I should like to say a word about the responsibility on both sides of this house. I should like also to say a word about the responsibility of a third side of parliament to which I shall refer in a moment. As for the two main sides that are here on the floor, the government and the opposition, I think we must face the fact that we have to do something about the element of time, not to save time so we can go home but to improve the use of our time so that we do not waste it on unimportant things. This, to me, is the essence of any proposal to save time in any particular phase of our procedure, not just to get through but to have a better apportionment of our time.
The Prime Minister made certain suggestions he thought should be considered. It is not necessary at this point to say what our views would be in respect of those specific suggestions. However, we are prepared to sit down with representatives of the various groups to study what the Prime Minister has suggested and ascertain if there are certain

things we could do even before the committee on procedure brings in its report. Undoubtedly what will have to be done will be to find ways of making better use of our time. Let it not be thought that the goal is simply to get home, that the goal is simply to cut down the amount of time that might be spent in the House of Commons.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, it is very easy to blame the other side. I think we have to look at both sides. I think we have to make a careful study, a study in depth to use a word that is commonly used today. In so far as the government is concerned, surely the government has the responsibility of introducing good legislation and planning the business of the house, of giving leadership in debate. The government's responsibility is to see to it that there are contributions made to the debate not only by those on the treasury benches but by those occupying the back benches as well. Parliament is not just an institution where the cabinet meets the opposition. Parliament consists of 265 members. 1 suggest that greater use should be made of all members of the house and there are ways in which this can be done.
On the opposition side of the house, we too have a responsibility. We have a responsibility not to block things that are good but to give them our support. We have a responsibility not just to stall for the sake of stalling. But we also have the responsibility to check everything that is brought in, to criticize where criticism is necessary; to examine expenditures and to examine legislation. We have a responsibility to prod the government where it fails to introduce legislation that it ought to be introducing. We are a major element in the whole parliamentary process.
May I take just a moment to refer to what to me is one of the most classic statements of the role of the opposition. It is found in Hansard for April 9, 1913, when Sir Wilfrid Laurier was setting out the role of the opposition. He referred, as will be found on pages 7433 and 7434, to the times in history, particularly in the British House of Commons, when the opposition, because it felt strongly on matters of public policy, did not hesitate to take time to try to prevent something being done that should not be done. I shall read a sentence or two from what Sir Wilfrid Laurier had to say:
On another occasion, in 1771, the majority of the house did not want to allow the publication of the debates. That strange position was opposed by a minority headed by no less a man than Edmund Burke, and Burke by whole days of obstruction succeeded in defeating the object of the majority, and, as he himself said afterwards, "posterity will bless the pertinacity of that day."
There are times, Mr. Speaker, when it is the duty of the opposition to talk and to do

its best to prevent certain things from getting through. It is the duty of the opposition to do this in the name of the people.
I see my time is fast running out, but I want to refer to a third side with respect to this matter of improving parliament. The third side, I suggest, relates to our friends in the press gallery. I want to suggest to them that I think they too have a responsibility. They enjoy, and we will protect it to the death, freedom to write about us as they choose. But I suggest that freedom carries with it responsibility, and that they should be interpreting what we are doing here to the Canadian people in the light of reasonable and valid standards. They should judge us not on the basis of whether they are tired because our speeches are lengthy; they should judge us not on some personal basis because they like this member or do not like that one or because they are in favour of the government or do not like a certain party. They should judge us in terms of what are the responsibilities of the government and the opposition. I invite my fellow members of all parties, government and opposition alike, to give serious thought to ways and means of improving parliament. I also invite our friends of the press gallery to join with us in trying to help make these improvements.
In these days Mr. Speaker, there take place a good many model parliaments in universities and other places. Some of us have had the privilege of attending some of them and performing certain functions. I think they are excellent. Out of this experience I should like to make a suggestion. I should like to suggest that some day when parliament can recess for a week or two, there be held in this chamber a model parliament par excellence. I propose that the members of it be the members of the press gallery. I make this proposal in all seriousness. I suggest we give them complete freedom to decide who is on the government side, who is on the opposition side, who are the cabinet ministers and who is the Speaker. We should give them complete freedom in every respect except one. I insist that if this model parliament is held, its members should treat it as though it were real, that they deal with the issues of the week they sit here as they come up and as if their function was real. Perhaps we could go up in the press gallery and we could write for the newspapers of Canada on how they perform.
It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, why I make this suggestion. I am asking that we try to improve the job we do here, but I am asking also that the members of the press gallery sit where we sit; that they look at parliament through eyes responsible to the Canadian people, and that they try to interpret it in the best way they possibly can
The Address-Mr. Addison so that some progress will be made toward what I believe is the ideal of all of us, toward what I believe the Canadian people want, toward what I believe we can have, not just a parliament that was glorious in history but a parliament today that carries out the full functions of democracy in doing a job for the Canadian people.

I should like to offer my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am sure their constituents can be proud of them. They certainly did justice to a very fine document. I should like also to congratulate the Prime Minister on his brilliant speech of yesterday. For one who has been in this chamber for only two parliaments it was the finest speech I have heard.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said, yesterday the Prime Minister suggested certain proposals to streamline and improve parliamentary procedure. I should like to follow the Prime Minister's lead and offer suggestions to the cabinet, particularly to the new Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickers-gill), in connection with an air policy for this country. As was mentioned in the speech from the throne, certain aspects of the Mac-Pherson royal commission report will be implemented in order to improve the operating efficiency of Canadian railways. This means that the time of the new Minister of Transport will be taken up largely by this legislation, as well as by the vast and complicated department that he has the privilege to head.
In the speech from the throne there was no specific mention of an over-all comprehensive air policy for Canada, but there was mention of other legislative proposals that may be coming before us this session. Without an over-all air policy I think the direction, the goals and the planning of this industry, and a very vital industry it is, are stunted. With a comprehensive air policy guide lines can be established which will take the matter out of the hands of the politicians.
I am sure all members of the house agree it is essential that this country should have a new aviation policy. It is needed now because of the apparent readiness of the United States to begin negotiations on trans-border

The Address-Mr. Addison routes. President Kennedy appointed Mr. J. K. Galbraith, former United States ambassador to India, to study trans-border routes between the United States and Canada, and after visiting Canada last summer he reported to the President. A copy of this report was also sent to the Prime Minister of Canada by Mr. Kennedy shortly before his assassination. While the contents of this report are confidential and secret, it is reported that a North American approach is recommended and that talks begin between the United States and Canada this spring. I suggest that this important question needs the attention of a full time minister, at least temporarily, to cover the whole field of aviation, telecommunication and meteorological services in this country.
Aviation policy should be broken down into three particular aspects. The first is international flag carriers, the second is transborder carriers and the third is domestic air carriers. My concern today is primarily with the international aspect of our air policy. As we are aware, international carriers are now in the process of reducing fares and are doing so very rapidly. I believe the next reduction goes into effect on April 1. This could be of serious consequence to our two flag lines operating out of Canada. In making his report to the railways, air lines and shipping committee the president of T.C.A., for example, pointed out that part of the profit realized on the trans-Atlantic runs was used to subsidize non-profit lines operating in Canada, as well as to cover part of the overall overhead.
This country must make a fundamental decision, namely whether a country of 19 million people can support more than one flag carrier internationally. Of the countries operating the more than 93 air lines which are members of the international air transport association, only three or four countries in the world operate more than one international flag carrier. These are notably the United Kingdom, the United States, France and Mexico. Looking at these countries we see that the United States, with a population of 180 million people, has four carriers, three of which are passenger and one cargo; namely Northwestern, Pan American, T.W.A. and Seaboard, which carries cargo only. Last year Pan American and T.W.A. attempted to merge but were prevented from doing so by the civil aeronautics board. Here we had a business decision overruled by a government body.
The United Kingdom has a population of 53 million people and has three international flag lines, B.O.A.C., B.E.A. and British Eagle.


B.O.A.C. and B.E.A. are government controlled and operated while British Eagle is a subsidiary of Cunard. B.O.A.C., as we know, has recently had a major shakeup of its senior personnel because of a poor operating statement, and the fact that it has been losing money steadily. France, with a population of 47 million people, operates three flag lines, Air France, T.A.I. and U.P.A., the latter for cargo only.
Ten flag carriers of other lands are authorized to land in Canada. These carriers have the right to pick up and deliver passengers in this country. So we can see that on what is called the blue ribbon run T.C.A. certainly is in intense competition.
My proposal is straightforward. I propose a merger for international purposes of Canada's two flag carriers. I would propose a merger along the lines of A.B.A., which represents Sweden in that country's participation in S.A.S. This merger should take place in the future on a timetable that will allow each air line to phase out duplicate personnel who would be eliminated by the merger. This would minimize any job dislocation.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, this idea is not new. It has been discussed for some time, particularly in 1962 when C.P.A. were operating at a very substantial loss. But the reasons for this proposal are very real. The first is that it would be a great aid to the government in negotiating bilateral agreements to negotiate for one air line representing Canada with one air line representing another country. When negotiating at the present time we negotiate on the basis of two for one.
This proposal would also eliminate wasteful competition between Canada's air lines internationally. I mean by that that in 1961 a route was granted to C.P.A. to fly from western Canada to London.
This route never came into existence because of the objection of the United Kingdom to landing rights for C.P.A. at London. But there is also the practice of booking passengers on other air lines when a sister Canadian company could provide that service. For example, at present T.C.A. is represented in Japan by Japan Air Lines. This means that would-be passengers for Toronto are carried by J.A.L. to Vancouver, via Hawaii and San Francisco and then onward by T.C.A. Canada misses the substantial foreign currency earnings that would be won if the Pacific flights were by a Canadian carrier.
With the advent of the new supersonic jet aircraft, and I am speaking specifically of the Concord and the new aircraft under development in the United States which will cost somewhere in the vicinity of $25 million


each, it will become increasingly difficult for private air lines to finance the purchase of aircraft like this. It is interesting to note that in a press	release which appeared in	theGlobe and	Mail	on February 16	referencewas made	to a	tentative order	given	byC.P.A. for	three	of these 2,000	miles	an
hour supersonic jet aircraft that are to be manufactured in the United States. That report read as follows:
C.P.A. said it was the only private enterprise air line in the delivery lineup that does not have some form of government subsidy available to it.
With a merger of the two air lines there would also be a reduction in sales staff and personnel throughout the world; but more important, a merger would ensure a private enterprise approach to the air line business, and I suggest that this is necessary under the conditions under which these two air lines are today operating in Canada.
We need only look at the last hearings of the committee on railways, air lines and shipping, held on Monday, December 2, 1963 to see what unfair competition the government sponsored line is operating under at present, and for an example of this I would like to quote from page 29 of that report:

During those hearings, which went on for four days, an official of the C.P.A. air line sat in attendance in the visitors' section of the committee room, and the full disclosure of T.C.A.'s position was placed before that committee for the information of its chief competitor.
There is also the question of political pressures brought to bear on management; for example, the political pressure brought to bear to keep the T.C.A. overhaul base in Winnipeg, which admittedly will cost T.C.A. a substantial amount of money, and the controversy that swirled throughout the House of Commons over the selection of short range jets, the DC-9 or the Caravelle. When these
The Address-Mr. Addison things happen it becomes increasingly difficult for a member of operating management to divorce himself completely from the political implications.
I suggest that when the air lines are in a healthy position, then this is the time to arrange for a merger. This should be a marriage of convenience and not of necessity. Nineteen sixty three was one of the best years international air lines ever enjoyed, and both Canadian air lines operated at a profit. Air lines in the United States operated at record earnings. Such a merger must be carried through in a spirit of co-operation. It is necessary so that an air line can operate as a business, and an air line must be conducted as a business with the minimum of interference from the government.
I do not think we should operate our flag line as an instrument of national prestige. I do not think it is unrealistic to look into the future when there may possibly be only 10 or 12 international flag carriers servicing all the nations of the world. As trade barriers are reduced competition will become more severe among competing air lines, and now is the time to lay our long range plans for an international flag line representing this country.
One may ask how a merger may be brought about. The heads of the two air lines have been competing against each other for some time and it is only natural that, as competitors, they would not advocate such a step. But I suggest it has worked successfully in other countries, and that it can work successfully here with the government and private industry in a fifty-fifty partnership in a national project. This would give the private enterprise approach with the aid of government financing.
I do not intend to go into a great deal of detail in connection with the merger of
S.A.S., but I think it is important that we look at part of it. S.A.S. is a company which represents Norway, Denmark and Sweden. Norway and Denmark each own two sevenths and Sweden owns the other three sevenths. The Swedish portion of this partnership is owned by a company called A.B.A., which company is controlled 50 per cent by private industry and 50 per cent by the Swedish government.
Each of these groups elects an equal number of directors to the board and the chairman of the board is appointed by the directors voting the government shares, but the operating executive committee is made up of four directors, two from private industry and two representing the government. The chairman of this operating executive committee is elected by the private interests.

The Address-Mr. Nielsen If a dividend is to be paid at the end of the fiscal year, it is determined by the group recommending the lowest figure.
I suggest that with co-operation between private and public financing a transportation company of this type could be a very valuable instrument for Canada, because with such a company as this Canada can utilize it in order to form her own merchant fleet. Today Canada has virtually no international merchant marine, and I think we have all accepted the fact that the country is not going to be in a position to manufacture highly sophisticated, large, supersonic transport aircraft. But we could build a merchant marine using Canadian shipyards, using Canadian personnel and material to build the ships, using Canadian men to man and sail them, and employ these vessels for the purpose of transporting Canadian agricultural products and manufactured goods originating here.
Any policy dealing with transportation is complicated because of regional interests involved. I suggest we accept that we must be united in order to compete internationally. I suggest we adopt a policy of co-operation between private industry and government whereby this company would be allowed to operate as a private company on a free enterprise basis.
This is a house of minorities, and some have accused us of timidity. I do not think this has been the case. Policies have been introduced into the house and pursued with vigour and courage. Courage will be needed to merge the air lines structure so as to form an over-all transportation complex. But for the good of the country and for the sake of competing internationally in the future I feel the approach must be one of full cooperation between government and private industry so as to develop one integral transportation company.
