speechtext:
I should like first of all to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address. They had a difficult task in attempting to make a mountain out of the molehill which that speech turned out to be.
In this regard I should like to say a word or two about the manner in which the Prime Minister treated the speech from the throne in the remarks he made. I think the Prime Minister's performance in his speech yesterday both before the supper recess and afterward was an amazing example of parliamentary irresponsibility. Here was a prime minister faced with a want of confidence motion based on his government's financial policy, a charge that the country was disillusioned with, and had rejected, the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and construction materials.

Yet he did not say one word about this 11 per cent sales tax. He did not deal with it at all, though this was the basis of the motion which faced him. Not one word was said by him in defence of his Minister of Finance or of the investment policy pursued by that hon. gentleman, although this subject was dealt with fully by the Leader of the Opposition.
The obvious reason for this, I suggest, is that the policies of the government in this regard are indefensible and the Prime Minister knows it. That is why he said nothing about them. It will be interesting to see whether any of the other cabinet ministers have anything to say about this particular subject if, indeed, they have the courage to attempt to defend these crippling financial policies.
Instead of addressing himself to this question the Prime Minister treated the house to a lecture from a text which, I would guess, had been prepared three or four weeks before the speech from the throne. It was a rehash of the throne speech itself. He talked about a magazine policy which had been previously announced by the Conservative government as though it were something entirely new. He said it did not really matter what the provincial premiers said about the pension plan. This is where the mask of diplomacy slips and the face of Liberal centralization peers forth. Hon. members opposite talk consultation, but they practice creeping centralization.
What has been the government's record in these last ten months, almost a year, and what has happened to that dynamic promise of a. blazing 60 days of action by the government? They have attempted to substitute diplomacy,, negotiation and dialogue for decision and action. They have negotiated from a position of weakness in pursuit of objectives which they have never been able to make clear even to themselves. In an irresponsible attempt to-twist the facts to fit preconceived theories, they have weakened confidence in Canada's, economy. They have embarked upon a series-of inept and ill advised measures based on emotionalism and political sloganeering rather than on a realistic appraisal of the situation.
Where are those promises made during the election campaign? They have disappeared during the last ten months and been replaced by a policy of postponement and evasion of the critical issues which must be resolved if we are to continue as a federal system. Hon. members opposite are surrounded now by the wreckage of their own frustrated endeavours. Relations with the provinces have deteriorated, to an all-time low level. Co-operative federalism, by which the government has set such store, has been reduced in effect to inoperative' Liberalism. Our relations with the United:.

States are no better. There is now a pathological fear of that country marked by subservience in the political field and defensiveness bordering on the neurotic in the economic field.
For ten months we have been afflicted with the weakest government since confederation. They are trying to be all things to all men. Pressure is bending them and opposition is buckling them. Vacillation and uncertainty are their watchwords. The rash election promises have backfired, and I intend to say a word or two about that diabolical dialogue of deception before I sit down. Decision has been supplanted by diplomatic dithering. Highly touted programs have had to be modified, withdrawn and revised in a series of humiliating retreats. The finest example of this is provided by the last budget brought down by the Minister of Finance. They have weakened the fabric and structure of confederation by dragging into the arena of partisan politics the relationship between the races and seeking to derive political advantage therefrom.
Now a word about the 11 per cent sales tax. This tax has, since its inception, met with a chorus of denunciation from industry, business and municipalities. It has had a marked restrictive effect on expansion. Now set at 4 per cent, it rises to 8 per cent on April 1 and 11 per cent on December 31. It was an ill conceived and incomprehensible measure. This is what the Prime Minister should have been dealing with in his reply to the motion of non-confidence moved by the Leader of the Opposition.
As to United States investment, the Minister of Finance says we need it, then he moves to turn off the tap. There is an almost psychopathic attitude toward the United States, a curious combination of hostility and servility. Every time the minister goes to Washington the policy changes. Financial houses, banks, the Quebec minister of finance, economists all across the country, claim that the Gordon anti-investment policy is unworkable and that we are cutting off our nose to spite our fiscal face.
The unworkability and ineptness of the policies of the present Minister of Finance throw strong doubt on his capacity to continue as minister. Obviously the hon. gentleman has no understanding of the workings of the economy, and refuses to accept the fact that the North American economy is an integrated economy and that measures designed to strike at the United States have a harmful effect on Canada's prosperity and on our ability to create new jobs for the growing working force. This is the gentleman who, during the last election campaign, said that
The Address-Mr. Nielsen one of the aims of the Liberal party in those blazing first 60 days of decision would be to pass measures to create full employment for all Canadians.
The reaction to the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and new equipment has been the most vitriolic of all so far as measures still in effect are concerned. The opposition has urged the government to repeal this tax because it has felt so deeply that it is retarding our national economic development. The 30 per cent tax had to be withdrawn. The withholding taxes are still causing friction in the United States and will probably be revised by the Minister of Finance. They should be, in any event.
The 11 per cent tax is still being subjected to a barrage of criticism from business and industry. I am sure all hon. members have received this sort of communication from businesses all across the country. The Canadian Lumbermen's Association, for instance, in a brief to the government on the 11 per cent sales tax called it a horrible and confusing mess, a state of complete confusion and uncertainty. They asked that the tax be removed. In its present form the tax is a pistol pointed at the head of business by this government, forcing expansion to take place before the rise to 11 per cent on December 31, 1964. The Liberals hope to have their cake and eat it too. They want to be able to point to the increase in building permits and construction as business attempts to get under the wire before the tax reaches the maximum. They have placed a one year deadline on expansion; that is the size of it. After December 31, 1964, they lower the boom with the full 11 per cent. It became a delayed action budget.
There has been no greater example of confusion and muddle-mindedness than the 11 per cent tax on building materials. First they put it on; then they withdrew it; then they were going to refund the money. Hon. members will remember what the Minister of Finance and the members on the treasury benches said when they spoke of this refund after pulling in their horns from 11 per cent to 4 per cent. They were going to refund to all suppliers the tax they had already been charged on building materials; but we have heard no more of those refunds.
The last budget was the most bitterly attacked budget in Canada's history. Bowing to public pressure, the government withdrew the budget piece by piece in the same way they are now doing with the pension plan. They have produced a diluted and watered down version of that plan. I think the Gordon budget, the 11 per cent sales tax, the 30 per cent withholding tax and all these other ill conceived measures might properly be termed

The Address-Mr. Nielsen frenzied financing. In a speech in Edmonton the minister said that large deficits should not be incurred in periods of prosperity and full employment. They have been telling us, particularly the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), that this is just such a period; the country is booming. At the same time the Minister of Finance says that we must have large deficits. Mr. Speaker, have you ever known such muddled thinking? The more they cut expenditures, the higher they get. We are faced in this country today with a deficit which will probably be the largest in Canada's peacetime history. The Minister of Finance, in Edmonton on January 28, had this to say:
I can properly report that as a result of a thorough examination and review, the estimates submitted by the civil departments and agencies of the government for next year have been cut by some $200 million.
In the very next paragraph of the report of the minister's remarks we find that he said the following:
This does not mean, of course, that in total they will be lower than for the current year. On the contrary, they must meet growing requirements and will therefore be higher.
What confusion and contradiction, Mr. Speaker. In the publication "Industry" published by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the issue for January, 1964, there appear these words:
Sales of manufactured goods by U.S.-owned companies based here totalled $9,6X0 million in 1962, of which $8,095 million represented sales made in Canada. But exports to the U.S. itself accounted for no less than $1,080 million, while exports to other countries brought in another $435 million.
Thus a substantial part of Canada's export trade, both to the United States and abroad, is provided by firms supported by foreign investment; yet we have a Minister of Finance who is doing all he can to curtail this type of investment. Through devaluation and the export drive we had produced a substantial improvement in the balance of payments situation, as the Minister of Finance himself admitted on more than one occasion. Outgoing payments in the shape of interest and dividend payments on foreign investment in 1962 represented 1.9 per cent of the gross national product, compared with 2.5 per cent of the gross national product in 1947. The figure remains substantial in so far as the balance of payments is concerned. Our method was to compensate by increasing exports and reducing imports, rather than by punitive measures which, if they do not kill the goose, will make him less eager to go on producing golden eggs for our benefit.
The Prime Minister in his remarks yesterday dealt with confederation. No government, in the short period they have been in power, has done more to impair confederation than

the government that is now sitting on the treasury benches. If there are strains on confederation they derive from the fact that for 30 years the Liberal party has persistently moved into fields of jurisdiction allocated to the provinces under the constitution. On his television program with Mr. Lynch and Mr. Claude Ryan of Le Devoir, the Prime Minister said that confederation was blurry. If it is blurry it is the Liberal party that has made it so. In his speeches the Prime Minister has talked about "reshaping confederation" and "writing a new chapter". It is not a reshaping that is needed, not a new chapter, but simply the restoration to the provinces of those rights taken away from them by the Liberal party over the years. In speech after speech the Prime Minister of Canada has cast doubt on confederation and confederation's capacity to survive.
Surely this talk of confederation being found wanting is not calculated to restore public confidence. Many Canadians who have a belief in Canada and Canada's future at least as strong and sincere as that of the Prime Minister are fed up to the teeth with this repeated suggestion that confederation has been found wanting. Throughout the remarks of the Prime Minister yesterday he spoke of a Canada from coast to coast, of a Canada from Atlantic to Pacific; he spoke of dominion-provincial conferences; he spoke of federal-provincial co-operation; but not once, sir, listening as carefully as I could, did I hear him refer to the one fully representative government above the sixtieth parallel and the legislative council of the Northwest Territories. Not once did he refer to those growing political bodies which are taking the first tottering steps toward full autonomy. Despite repeated requests throughout last session-and they will be made again this session-not one inch has been given by the government in agreeing to the suggestion that in these conferences and consultations where provincial-territorial plans are discussed there should be representation by the two territories. There are taxpayers in the north; there are forms of government in the north, and if any contributions are to be made to pension plans and other plans where provincial-federal co-operation is required, then certainly the territories should be consulted. They signed the same kind of fiscal agreement with the federal government as the provinces signed, and they have the same spheres of jurisdiction, legislatively, as provinces, with only three exceptions.
All that is required, I suggest, is a reversal of the Liberal policies of centralization which have warped and twisted the idea of confederation into a form that is now barely recognizable. The present government, made

up as it is of the inheritors of the policies of Mackenzie King and his then secretary, the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickers-gill), is hardly the instrument to bring this about. Give back to the provinces, I say to the government, their historic rights and you will hear no more talk about confederation being found wanting. Give them the capacity to secure the financial resources necessary for the development of provincial resources, the funds necessary to meet the mounting costs of education. Then you will have an end to the uncertainty and confusion which more than anything else are at the base of the present problem.
The overlapping in the field of welfare as exemplified by the pension plan is not only a case in point but the best example which could be discussed at this time. This government wants a pension plan, and it went at it like a bull at a gate. It began by antagonizing the two provinces without whose co-operation it would be impossible to have a pension plan. It did not consult; it had a theory, and then tried to twist the facts to fit that theory.
This has been its course in every sphere, Mr. Speaker. The premier of Quebec came here and said there was no consultation on municipal loans, pensions, depressed area legislation; and I feel, as I charged last session, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) knew at the time of the feelings of the premier of Quebec and that he was going to introduce a pension plan, yet boldly presented her pension plan to this House of Commons without disclosure of that fact.
The former government was never in that position, because the provinces were respected and were consulted. The chaos and confusion in welfare on the federal-provincial and municipal levels can only be resolved through national welfare consultation at which the lines of authority will be set out, and the costs allocated and the jurisdictions defined. The business of having plans cooked up in the inner recesses and back rooms of the Liberal party and then shoved down the throats of the provinces on a take it or leave it basis is a dead end street. We all remember how fond they were of that course of action prior to 1957; apparently they have not yet learned their lesson.
On January 11 the Prime Minister wrote the provincial premiers and told them that because Quebec was adopting its own pension plan, age-reduced benefits will be financed from the existing old age security fund rather than from the Canada pension plan. The old age security fund is financed from taxes, whereas the Canada pension fund is to be financed from contributions. In spite of the
The Address-Mr. Nielsen Prime Minister's statement that payments before 70 will be financed from taxes, we have the Minister of Finance speaking in Edmonton on January 28 and saying this:
This plan will be fully self-supporting from contributions to be made by those covered by it and from their employers, just as private pension plans are.
The Prime Minister wrote the premiers on January 11 setting out the details of the watered down version. In the memorandum he sets out as one of the essential features of the plan that it will be universal. On the same page of that memorandum to the provincial premiers he says they are now willing to revise this consideration. It can hardly be a universal plan, sir, without the co-operation of one of the most important provinces in the country.
I am in agreement with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that the Liberals have no monopoly on the idea of a universal contributory pension plan. At the time the government changed we were negotiating with the provincial governments and were attempting to obtain agreement on amendments to the British North America Act so as to be able to provide for survivor benefits within the framework of the universal contributory plan. All this was on the basis of the recommendations contained in the Clark report. The Liberals in fact likely stole from the Clark report the plan which they are now endeavouring to force through the house.
This is a highly technical and complex subject which could not possibly have been worked out between the time the Liberals took office and the time the minister of health and welfare made her announcement in the house. When we were in office departmental officials were working on a plan for two years. As to delay, this is simply the result of trying to obtain a plan which would meet the approval of all the provinces and required negotiations with those provinces. That was a plan which has not been followed by this government, which is why they are coming to grief in attempting to get acceptance of it. Compare this to the Liberal approach now, where the provinces were not consulted until late last year, months after the plan was announced as ready to be transformed into law; and it was not until January of this year that the Prime Minister's letters to the provincial premiers were released.
The reaction to the Liberal plan is almost universal rejection, with the province of Quebec embarking on a plan of its own and Ontario accepting conditionally, and this before the details were even known. All that appears to be left of the plan after almost universal rejection is a catch phrase which

The Address-Mr. Nielsen would be appealing to the electorate, especially if the Liberals in their usual fashion were to be able to fix the opposition with the responsibility for their own neglect and in the face of having their plan rejected by the provinces. We had been working with the provinces for two years and would have continued to do so in order to work out a method of implementing a pension plan before asking parliament to make it law. That is what the government should have done in this case, and the blame for their coming to grief rests with them alone.
I now want to deal, Mr. Speaker, in the time left to me with what I call a diabolical dialogue. The Prime Minister is fond of the term "dialogue". I went through some election pamphlets and material published by the Liberal party in the last election campaign, and I am going to go through some of the promises which were made. In each case the result of the promise has been nil, but I think it desirable that they be on the record.
The first promise: Improve social security in a responsible way that will make it an aid to economic growth. In particular, institute a medicare plan, improve unemployment insurance and establish portable contributory pensions. The result to date: Nothing.
The promise: Reorganize the international development bank as a development corporation co-operating with private enterprise to provide capital for industrial extension. The result: Nothing.
The promise: Give leadership in research, especially for the processing of more Canadian materials in Canada. The result: Nothing.
The promise: Promote policies for freer trade by co-operating constructively and energetically with other free world countries to reduce barriers and expand trade. The result: Nothing.
The promise: In co-operation with the provinces, to see that more low rental homes are built. The result: Nothing.
The promise: In federal contracts, cover increased costs of work done in the winter. The result: Nothing.
The promise: Put federal contributions to municipal winter works on a sliding scale, carefully supervised and rising to the whole of labour costs in areas of severe and chronic unemployment. The result: Nothing.
The promise: Improve federal legislation to speed up conciliation procedures. The result: Nothing.
The promise: To restore the unemployment insurance fund, extend its coverage, and return it to its proper use. The result: Nothing.
The promise: To pay unemployment insurance benefits to people who are out of work because of illness. The result: Nothing.

The promise: Improve retraining and pay supplementary benefits in cases of long term unemployment. The result: Nothing.
The promise: To vigorously promote sound projects for northern development. The result: Nothing.
The promise: Study of ways to sell and use coal will have a prime priority in our Atlantic development plan. The result: Nothing.
The promise: To restore term 29 to the terms of confederation. The Minister of Transport will be interested in that one. The result: Nothing.

I am quoting from a promise which was made in St. John's, Newfoundland, on March 22, 1963, during the last election campaign, when the Liberals promised to restore term 29 to the terms of confederation, and after ten months have done nothing about it.
The promise: A review of civil defence policy. The result: Nothing. Not only that, but there will likely be greater expenditures than ever before, and in addition the minister of defence has decimated the militia, which was the nucleus of our civil defence force in this country.
The promise: Freer trade with Caribbean countries and even closer commercial and financial arrangements. The result: Nothing.
The promise: Extend family allowances to children beyond the age of 16; that is for boys and girls who remain at school. The result: Nothing.
The promise: A system of bursaries which would be repayable to help young persons obtain university education. I presume that is the scholarships promise. The result: Nothing.
The promise: Extension of and increase in federal grants for urban renewal in order to remove slums. The result: Nothing.
The promise: During those blazing 60 days of decision, to reduce the federal voting age to 18. The result: Nothing.
The promise: The Liberal party's portable pension plan can be introduced at once, since it involves no added expenditure by the federal government. The result: Nothing. Where did the portability of that pension plan disappear to in the explanations we have heard of this pension plan?
The promise: It is a firm commitment of the Liberal party to introduce a national health plan in its first term. The result: Nothing.

The promise: "I am confident that a medical care plan can be introduced in the first parliament of a Liberal administration." The result: Nothing.
The promise: A careful review of all high tariff rates with a view to their reduction or removal. The result: Nothing. There is a withholding tax now, Mr. Speaker, and there is also a plan to put an additional 15 per cent tax on aircraft imported into this country, that is light aircraft.
The promise: Immediate action to hard surface the gravel air strip at Deek lake, Newfoundland. The Minister of Transport should pay attention to this one. The result: Nothing.
The promise: Assistance for Elliot Lake, Ontario, and this is something to which the Prime Minister should give attention. The result: Nothing.
The promise: Construction of deep water ports along the St. Lawrence river in the Rimouski area as part of the Liberal party's area development program, and winter navigation across the river to the north shore. The result: Nothing.
The promise: Payments of 90 per cent of the cost of completing the trans-Canada highway, completion of engineering studies of the Chignecto canal and the Prince Edward Island causeway, and use of native coal for the production of electric power. The result: Nothing.
The promise: Increased assistance to the gold mining industry. The result: Nothing.
The promise: An inland waterway from Montreal to Georgian bay following the Ottawa river. The result: Nothing.
The promise: More air strips and radio communications for the north. The result: Nothing.
The promise: Immediate paving of the Alaska highway. The result: Nothing.
The promise: "Our whole task is to narrow the cost of living for those who fight the north." This is the minister of northern affairs speaking. "We should use public funds to make it economic for investment and risk capital to enter the country." He should get together with the Minister of Finance. The result: Nothing.
The promise: Reduced costs of transportation and communication through more air strips and roads; faster tax write-offs and extension of the three year tax free period now allowed for new mines. Again this is the minister of northern affairs speaking. The result: Nothing.
This, sir, is the diabolical dialogue of deception. If I had been allowed more time for research, if I had had more than the one hour I spent in going through the Liberal promises, I could be speaking here for the
The Address-Mr. Marcoux next week cataloguing this phony list of promises, weaving this fabric of chicanery that was offered to the people of this country and which bamboozled them into voting that party into power. This government is now frittering it all away. This is the program which the Canadian people had a right to expect would be put in effect, Mr. Speaker. Shylock's students on the treasury benches had better take a second look at their promises made during the last election campaign.

speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne as well as those who have recently become cabinet ministers, and those whose transfer to another department enabled them to gain new fame.
I also would particularly commend the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) for the very fine speech he made earlier today, which was similar in trend to those of the mover and the seconder of the address in reply. The one unfortunate thing, is that there is often a long way to go from words to action.
The "giant" from the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) just told us so-and I think he might strike his own breast and confess that, during the five years that his government was in power, the result of various problems he tackled was nought, zero, exactly like the nought he is trying to charge to the Liberal party at this time.
There is even some hope that politics will not always be a matter of going one better than the other old party in the way of election promises, with the idea that they will never be carried out, and trusting that the government will be long enough in power to make the voters forget that it failed to keep its word. There is nothing new in that respect, because it has been always so since 1867.
If Providence allows us to celebrate the centenary of confederation, we shall at the same time celebrate the centenary of the electoral promises which were made by the old-line parties and which have not been kept.
As usual, the speech from the throne is a pretty dull document, which says little. On the other hand, it showed the centralizing propensity of the Liberal party. The speech from the throne also allowed us to recognize the architect of the Liberal party's policy for some years, that is the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne). What is bred in the bone will come out in the flesh.
Previously, the provinces were robbed of
their privileges, they were not consulted, they

The Address-Mr. Marcoux were at some time informed that due to a national emergency the federal government was forced to deprive them of the rights to which they were entitled under the constitution, more precisely by the spirit and the letter of confederation.
Today, the behaviour is more proper. The provinces are advised that they will again be deprived of their privileges, but this, after consultation. It is said that the federal government is forced to take such action, which is contrary to provincial autonomy, but that the individual governments of the provinces will be informed before action is taken.
In regard to students' loans, this is a flagrant example showing to what degree, despite nice words from the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), from the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), the government does exactly the opposite of what it says. The Prime Minister admitted he had not consulted the provinces in the case of assistance to students, more specifically in regard to interest free loans to students.
He indulged in fine rhetorics which could be termed as diplomatic since he is quite able in that field. But if you look for the answer to that question, you realize that he had not consulted the provinces.
As for the other centralizing measures they are trying to put through, it is specifically said in the speech from the throne that the provinces will be consulted. The procedure is always the same. It was followed by the Conservative government since 1957 and it has always been followed by the Liberal government in the past. The provinces are put before an accomplished fact.
When it was contemplated to set up a hospital insurance plan, the provinces were told: if you wish the federal government to pay 50 per cent of hospital expenditures, you will have to accept the plan as proposed.
The provinces were not asked for their views, and especially not the "belle province" which, at that time, did not have the honour and the privilege of being under the leadership of Mr. Lesage. But if that province had been asked under what terms it would join the hospital insurance plan, I think we could have had a more equitable plan for the province of Quebec.
And if I refer to the province of Quebec, it is because I live there. But the situation is the same in the other provinces. The point is not to discriminate in favour of Quebec. That is not at all a question of Quebec receiving a handout. I am talking about the autonomy of the provinces generally.
And when the present premier of the province of Quebec, Mr. Lesage, accepted the hospital insurance plan on January 1,

1961, he accepted a joint program. As a matter of fact, he accepted it unconditionally and went so far as to say that the people of Quebec were taking the Union Nationale party to task for having previously refused to share in a joint program.
Now, as you can see, the two old-line parties, in the federal as much as in the provincial field, have a great deal to be ashamed of and neither of them has any lesson to take from the other. We always hear a lot of fine talk, but good things are always much more easily said than done. I shall come back to this in a moment.
Another measure mentioned in the speech from the throne has to do with the retirement of senators. I feel that is a step in the right direction. It is obvious that, having reached a certain age, some people are no more useful in a legislative body than they would be elsewhere. And the fact remains that they are entitled to quite an attractive pension for the work they may have done.
Nevertheless, I believe other changes should be made in the act amending the Senate.
Personally, I find it improper for the Senate to be a refuge for people who are caught in the act. In my opinion, it is not right to reward somebody who pleads guilty to certain charges after having previously denied them. But this person is rewarded by being appointed to an office that is not only fairly well paid, but in which he is protected from the fury of the Canadian voters.
It would be possible, it seems to me, to have at least half the senators appointed by the provinces and the other half perhaps by the party in office. This would be a more judicious procedure. A little later on it might be advisable to improve the quality of senators by selecting them from among intermediate bodies, which are so important these days, such as employers' associations, labour unions, professional organizations, etc. Those people are generally competent and would be appointed by their respective bodies. Therefore, instead of abolishing the Senate, it might be possible to improve it, because I feel that it could then render very valuable services.
The speech from the throne also refers to the redistribution of electoral districts. Theoretically, from a demographic and geographic point of view, such a measure should certainly prove advantageous in a democratic country.
However, it was found in the last byelections that the greater the population of a city, the fewer members of parliament it needs, because the people are less interested in public matters. Therefore, when a redistribution of electoral districts is being considered and would be likely to increase the

number of urban ridings compared to rural ridings, I feel that there would be some danger of injustice, because the problems of a city, of a great urban centre are pretty much the same, and having a great number of members will not solve those problems. And in proof of this, there is the example set recently by the voters in Montreal.
I do not blame them, because apparently they had agreed that it was not worth taking the trouble to vote for the political parties represented. And it is not because the Rallie-ment Creditistes did not get enough votes that the people did not bother to vote. It is because they thought that it was not worth taking the trouble to support that political party. In addition, with the organization set up by the Ralliement and since all the Creditistes did vote, I am convinced that they obtained more than their share.
But it means that people are no longer interested in politics, especially in a city like Montreal. Such a fact was noted, when the mayor of Montreal was elected by a considerable majority, while only 25 or 30 per 100 of voters went to the polls.
In my opinion, such a fact should be taken into consideration when the redistribution of the electoral districts is studied. I agree that the population should be taken into account. But there are also many other factors showing the democratic spirit of our government still better than certain political considerations which should not be disregarded.
The speech from the throne also announced a measure to control electoral expenditures. There will at least be something in our legislation to show that political parties are aware that electoral expenses are exceptionally high and that it is easy for a party to cheat on unreported expenditures.
Apart from recognizing that principle, I think that this step will be to no avail, because nothing will prevent political parties from establishing electoral funds outside the scope of the regulations prescribed in the legislation. However, and once again, it is an attempt to bring about a solution to a problem which will remain very hard to solve in a democracy.
I note that in the speech from the throne, mention was made of the O'Leary report on publications. That legislation was to be introduced by the Conservative government in 1963 but they saw fit not to do so. At the time I knew that the legislation which was going to be presented would grant special privileges to two U.S. magazines, Time and Reader's Digest. In fact, we know that those two magazines are about the only ones which
The Address-Mr. Marcoux could be detrimental to Canadian publications. A regulation is made in order to stop advertising in all U.S. magazines which are not harmful to Canadian magazines and we allow the cost of advertising published in these two U.S. magazines, which really do some harm to our Canadian magazine industry, to be deducted.
I am of the opinion that, once again, this is only window dressing. The government wants to give the impression that it looks after Canadian industries when, in fact, it does not worry about them at all. As a matter of fact, it takes care of the people liable to contribute, even just a little, to its slush funds. That is why I say that the proposed change, which follows one of the recommendations made in the O'Leary report, is not enough. Instead of protecting Canadian magazines, I feel that it will hurt them.
Mr. Speaker, other measures could have been included in the speech from the throne but they were not, and there is not a hint about them.
There is in my district a naval yard which is very well equipped and has highly skilled workers who have proved themselves in the construction of war ships, frigates, destroyers, etc.
I am convinced that the government should ecourage this shipyard. Let me say right away that I have in mind the shipyard in Lauzon, because there is another one in my riding, in St. Laurent, on Orleans island, which practically had to close because of the lack of interest of governments which did not give it any business either for naval ships or for merchant ships. In my opinion, if there is an industry which should be protected and maintained in that area, it is indeed the Lauzon shipyard.
And if an atomic submarine should be built, as it has been implied, I think it should be built in that area and in that shipyard. Calling for tenders in foreign countries is an idea that should not even be entertained. Mention has been made of possible tenders from Japan, Scotland or England.
I know that in some cases tenders have to be called for abroad but when it comes to construction of this type, in which we are interested, I believe that tenders should be restricted to this country, regardless of the fact that it could cost a little more. The money would at least remain in this country and would be put into circulation among our people.
Many individuals would get employment and would thus pay income taxes; we would then be able to recoup a good deal of the amounts made available to these firms for shipbuilding, while we do not save anything by having this work done abroad. Apart from

The Address-Mr. Marcoux
not saving anything, we are always obliged to assign part of the budget to social assistance for unemployed people, who cannot pay income tax any more.
While I am on the subject of income tax,
I would like to return to the matter of charitable receipts. This question has been discussed at length and I know that some newspapers published in English, in other provinces, seemed to insinuate that the people of Quebec were deducting maliciously or improperly certain taxable amounts through charitable receipts. Well, I believe that these statements have been made without any knowledge of the facts, and I am sure that the people of Quebec are in every way as honest and righteous as the citizens of the other provinces. If, in other provinces, people do not take full advantage of these allowable deductions, it is that they find other means, and, in the end, their net income is still higher than that of the citizens of the province of Quebec. Either the government should accept the 10 per cent deduction for charitable donations or it should strike out from our statutes the provision concerning that deduction. I submit that the government should increase the basic exemptions in the field of income tax to enable the people to eke out their small salaries.
I should now like to say a few words about the all-Canadian games which are to be held in the province of Quebec. This question has already been raised by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) and several others. We were given to understand that the government would make grants for amateur sports. I feel such grants should be made in particular to interprovincial games. That had to wait until the cabinet was reshuffled, until the session was opened, until the speech from the throne was written. I wonder what we are waiting for now. The session is now in full swing and the organizers of these games no longer know where they stand; they wonder whether the games should be held on schedule since they have not yet received the contribution they should normally get from the federal government. The only thing the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) said was that the question was under advisement and that the parties concerned would be informed of the decision in due course.
I submit that the question is urgent, that the government is able to make a contribution and that it should make its decision known as soon as possible, especially since it claims to reach decision promptly when it is faced with problems.
I come now to a point which has already been mentioned by spokesmen for the Con-

servative party, the 11 per cent tax on building materials. This tax is detrimental to the whole Canadian building industry. The link between construction and employment is such that when construction is hampered, employment goes down and unemployment goes up.
I regret that the editor of Le Soleil is not in the house because he could say that I have just made a truism. However, when one does not state self-evident truths, people do not seem to understand why there is unemployment. Coming back to the tax in question, I say that it is detrimental to construction in general and to employment in particular. What in theory is supposed to reduce unemployment actually increases it.
Hence I believe the government is in a position to remove this 11 per cent tax. They will have to do it before long because the industry will find itself in dire straits.
I wish now to come to another question concerning eastern farmers. Despite what the Prime Minister said, the whole of eastern Canada is now fully aware that the party in office, as the one before it, is not interested in eastern agriculture and does not look after it. That has become obvious. They have tried to disguise this attitude under other names, other sentences, other manoeuvres. We in Quebec realize, as well as people from the other eastern provinces, that agriculture does not seem to interest the government at all, not because it is not a paying proposition economically, but because it is not so politically. In the province of Quebec, people always end up voting for the Liberal party even though the government does not look after the farmers.
In the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, the same ideas prevail, and even if there is no involvement of specific assistance to agriculture, their citizens always find other motives to cast their votes in favour of the old parties. So, I suggest that although it is not necessary for political purposes to give assistance to the farmers of eastern Canada, the government should nevertheless do so in a very specific manner. The present Minister of Agriculture is incapable of answering questions pertaining to western Canada. How can we hope to have him answer those concerning the agricultural conditions of eastern Canada?
As far as the new minister of forestry and rural development is concerned, we know what this means. We are under the impression that the farmers of eastern Canada are not any better off than they were before.
I should like now to say a word about nuclear weapons. Many people have dealt with the question. Those are very dangerous

weapons which could cause massive destruction of people. This is a truth recognized by everybody. Although x-rays, smoking and drinking are also very dangerous, this does not mean that we have to make all those things disappear because they are dangerous. In the same way, the country needs to defend itself. The North American territory needs to take up to date measures and not try to defend itself with bayonets as in 1914. However, when we are offered weapons which are obsolete, which are not worth anything and which cost millions of dollars, the best thing to do is not to accept them. It is not a question of saying that we want or do not want the Bomarcs, it is a question of saying that we must not spend money on futile things so long as there is no evidence that nuclear weapons are indispensable and we have the means to buy them.
In my opinion, the government must oppose the acquisition and the storing of nuclear arms. Moreover, Social Credit urged before last session the setting up of an independent defence committee.
Well, that committee was appointed and worked wonderfully under a very able chairman, maybe not in the field of defence, but as far as the set-up of the committee was concerned. All the members of that committee were in earnest and I can say so because I was not one of them. Those people are now in a position to assess what Canada's defence policy should be, and when that committee brings forward a complete report, I think its suggestions should be accepted because investigations were carried out very seriously.
I should also like to say a few words on the non-confidence motion introduced by the Conservative party. People are being led to think that those who vote against that motion are in favour of the 11 per cent tax.

But some reporters and radio or television commentators have succeeded, by sleight-of-hand tricks which might be also diplomatic- probably inspired by our politicians-in hoodwinking people into believing that when you
The Address-Mr. Marcoux vote for or against an amendment, it means you are for or against the wording of the amendment, which is not so.
If the amendment is ruled out by Mr. Speaker, and the question is put with regard to that amendment, the vote will not be on the amendment itself but on the validity of the amendment and on Mr. Speaker's ruling. The members of the press gallery succeeded in convincing the public of the opposite.
Yesterday, on television, I listened to a French speaking commentator whom I shall not name. According to him it was understood that the splinter parties would do some bargaining in 1964, as they had done in 1963.
Another newspaperman whom I have to name because I think that his chronicle is always neither fish nor fowl; he begins by bludgeoning his man and ends on a flattering note, or else he starts by building him up to knock him down in the end. I am speaking of Poliquin of L'Action who states that:
Mr. R. N. Thompson's Social Credit group is unable to make a significant contribution to this federal session. Because of some agreement which remains secret, they will continue to support the Liberal government-

We shall vote in favour of the Conservative amendment, not because it tends to abolish the 11 per cent tax, but to show to all those who make such insinuations that we are quite capable of assuming our own responsibilities before our voters and the general public, and that we need nobody's advice in this respect.
Indeed it is hardly surprising that those people take such an attitude. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to make a few remarks concerning the implementation of the report of the MacPherson royal commission.
The Liberal government came to power with a promise by the Prime Minister to a nation-wide radio and television audience that our party would bring before the Canadian people new and imaginative policies. I believe we have done that. They would be policies which would lift this country out of the doldrums-and we are doing this-and make for a happier and fuller life for all our citizens. Many Canadians, including supporters of other parties, were impressed by that promise and took it seriously. To forget about it and continue in the same old way of doing things would leave us undistinguishable from the Conservatives. And, I would say, it might cost us a working majority at the next election.
During the years when the Conservatives were in power-and I am talking about the period 1957-1963-they had no national policy for dealing with our national transportation problems. The railways are the biggest problem in the transportation field. Whether it was a freight rate increase or a wage increase, the Conservatives had no answer but to tack on another subsidy. When they had finished the job they had added a total of $70 million per year to the total subsidies being paid to the railways; $20 million to hold down freight rates and $50 million to meet the wage increase in 1961. We have the job of sorting out this mess.
One of the industries that was infuriated by the railway policies of the Conservatives was, as hon. members well know, the trucking industry. I happen to know some people

in that industry. Some of the strongest voices that were raised against the policies of the Diefenbaker government were those of the leading Conservatives in the industry, and some of them actively supported us in the last election. Hon. members also know that while the Conservatives were busy putting on new subsidies for the railways they had a royal commission on transportation investigating the transportation problem. This was the MacPherson commission. Mr. Speaker, this commission came out with recommendations which, if they are put into effect, will cost the taxpayers of Canada $100 million in subsidies in the first year. Hon. members are well aware that this also drew a very adverse reaction from the trucking industry.
Another thing that greatly worried the trucking industry about the MacPherson commission report was the recommendation that most of the regulation of transport, including the regulation of trucking, should end. The third thing that worried this industry was the recommendation of the commission that the railways should be allowed to operate at will in the highway transport field.
The trucking industry filed briefs against these recommendations with both the previous government and the present government. However, Mr. Speaker, in reading the statements of senior officers of the industry it can be seen they appreciate that the MacPherson commission recommendations on subsidies are on a declining, self liquidating basis. To their credit the industry leaders, in their own meetings, have made every effort to make the industry realize that if railway subsidies have to continue, it is much better to put up with subsidies that decline annually rather than have subsidies that go on forever at the same rate. Indeed, under the Conservatives the trucking industry had every reason to believe that the subsidies would get bigger, not smaller.
I think it might be well if we stopped right here and looked for a moment at the trucking industry. There are well over 10,000 trucking companies in Canada. They range all the way from the smallest to the largest truck operators. About 6,000 of this number are represented in the membership of Canadian trucking associations. They account for close to 90 per cent of the trucking equipment that is operated. There are approximately 100,000 employees of the industry, including terminal employees and drivers. This is no small part of the labour force of Canada.
From reading the industry magazines that come into my office I can see that the people in the industry are worrying a great deal about their public image. They may have
The Address-Mr. Foy
reason to do so. Nevertheless, I think it should be recognized that the vast majority of people in this industry are responsible businessmen. They work hard; they have the same problems in obtaining capital to finance their businesses as anyone else; they survive and expand by providing a public service. If they fail to do that job properly, they go out of business; there is no federal government to come along and help them or tide them over another crisis.
An increasing number of trucking executives are prominent members of local service clubs, boards of trade, chambers of commerce, the community chest, and so on. Thousands of dollars are being contributed by the industry in Ontario and Quebec to needy students through contributions placed in their hands through the universities. The industry knows that despite its large labour force, one of the largest single groups of employees in Canada, it does not "register", from the employee standpoint, with federal politicians. The people in this industry trace this to two causes. The first is that the industry is partly unionized and partly not unionized, and even where unionization exists-and this takes in all the larger companies-there is not one large union group, as in the case of the railway brotherhoods, but a large number of locals of the same union spread all across Canada.
The second cause of political indifference to the trucking labour force is that of the unions the trucking industry does have, the teamsters account for about 95 per cent of the union membership. The trucking industry knows that it cannot rely on any imagined or political strength radiating from the teamsters; the reputation of that union south of the border takes care of that. On the other hand, the industry sees that the railway brotherhoods, despite shrinking employment on the railways, still have an attentive ear in the governments of Canada.
However, many trucking companies have company newspapers and bulletins which go to all their employees, briefing them on the problems that the industry faces. Therefore many thousands of trucking employees are becoming aware of what the trucking industry regards as its problems federally. In addition many goodwill meetings of employees are called by the management of the different trucking companies, and at these meetings the employees are briefed on the problems the industry feels it is up against.
For example, the other night in Montreal there was a large meeting of truck drivers, followed by a reception, which was attended by senior representatives of the trucking industry associations, the associations of the owners, not only from the province of Quebec

The Address-Mr. Foy
but from Ottawa as well. At this meeting more than $5,000 in cheques was distributed to drivers who had good safety records and who had passed the St. John's ambulance course. I am told that at the reception afterward the senior association representatives passed among the drivers discussing with individual groups the fact that this is an industry and that all who make up the industry, whether they own the trucks or drive them, have a stake in its future and in fair government treatment of it.
If the dominion bureau of statistics figures indicate the correct story, the total investment in the Canadian trucking industry is well over $1 billion. A few weeks ago the former minister of transport, Hon. George Mcllraith, was quoted as saying that the Liberal government would soon announce a national air line policy for Canada. To the best of my knowledge the Liberal government

indeed, any federal government-has never announced a policy for the trucking industry of Canada; yet parliament has jurisdiction over the entire international and interprovincial section of the industry, which is a very large part of the industry. Thus it has responsibility for what happens to the industry by reason of existing federal policies.
The investment in the Canadian air line industry, including T.C.A., C.P.A. and all the other scheduled commercial air lines, does not begin to approach the more than $1 billion of investment in the Canadian trucking industry. So right away I begin to wonder, where does the government stand in bringing together a national transportation policy for Canada. I have every confidence that this government will do so. However, to date it has said nothing about a national trucking industry policy.
One may say that this is not a new situation, that it has been going on for years. I do not think anyone in the Liberal party should take the negative attitude that what went on in the years under the Conservatives makes a continuation of the situation under the Liberals justifiable. Surely it should be the opposite. I notice that in volume III of the report of the MacPherson royal commission, which is the volume containing a number of special studies conducted at the direction of the commission, a consulting economist, Dr. E. W. Carr of Ottawa, made this statement which appears at page 90:
The federal government has been so little involved with highway transport that it has not been concerned either with policy in this field or to a sufficient extent with the substantial range of information which would be needed to develop .an effective federal policy. It is notable that the first recognition of the trucking industry in federal legislation came only on June 9, 1961.

The closing of the door in the face of the trucking industry by the federal government in the past is action difficult to understand. In the submission of the Liberal government of Quebec to the MacPherson royal commission on transportation it was stated that:
Transportation policies are largely national policies....The government of the province of Quebec stands ready to co-operate with the other provinces and the federal government in the development of transportation policies which will best serve the interests of all Canadians.
That quotation can be found at pages 65 and 66 of the submission of Quebec to the MacPherson commission. Yet this development of a national transportation policy has not materialized. There can be no claim truly made that a national transportation policy exists when the Canadian trucking industry has never been a part of that policy.
When Mr. John Magee, the executive secretary of the Canadian trucking associations, was being examined before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines on December 13, 1962 he was asked about continuation of the 1959 subsidy of $20 million to the railways, and he replied, as reported at page 138 of the proceedings:
Well, we suggest you reject the legislation. When we first appeared we were met with the problem, well, it is only going to be one year, and now we are met with the statement that it is only going to be a little while until the MacPherson recommendations come into effect, so they ask us to hang on a little longer. One other thing: I do not feel in all the years I have appeared before this committee that I really have made very much of an impression on behalf of the trucking industry.
To this the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner) replied "But you have". Mr. Magee's answer was:
I wonder why the truckers send me back. I invited them not to do so this year. I just wanted to say, Mr. Chairman, that I still cannot understand why, after all these years, the parliament of Canada will not recognize this industry and take into account its problems in the consideration it gives to these matters.
The trucking industry has asked for permission to make submissions to the government, and these submissions have been made. But one cannot claim that merely permitting an industry to make a submission means the government has recognized it. Recognition occurs only if there is tangible evidence in the national transportation policy of Canada that there is a trucking industry and that the industry is not ignored in any measure that affects it directly.
I have spoken about the trucking industry's reaction to the $100 million in subsidies recommended for the Canadian railways in the MacPherson report. I have also expressed a belief based on what I can get from the industry's statements, that they might feel

that something had been gained if such subsidies were spelled out as declining, self liquidating subsidies, as recommended in the MacPherson report.
With regard to the two other recommendations in the MacPherson report to which the trucking industry objected strongly-and I refer to the removal of most regulations on transportation, and to the recommendation that the railways be allowed to enter at will into the field of highway transportation-the industry does see in the MacPherson report certain qualifying recommendations. This is clear from a careful reading of the industry's statements that have appeared, from the president of Canadian trucking associations, Mr. D. A. Chapman, and others.
For example, the commission recommended that where such subsidies as the Maritime Freight Rates Act continue to be paid, truck shipments as well as rail shipments should be included, giving the shipper a free choice of transportation agencies. Another such subsidy is the federal feed grain freight assistance subsidy, paid only on rail and water shipments, which the MacPherson commission found not only discriminated against the trucking industry but discouraged the use of the lowest cost transportation agency. The government announced on August 22 that a new federal feed freight assistance policy would be adopted and that truck shipments henceforth would be included. This policy has not yet been implemented.
Turning to the question of unrestricted entry of the railways into the trucking field, it is to be noted that the commission's view that this was desirable was qualified by the recommendation that railway regulations in Canada should require that the accounts of railways and railway-owned truck lines be completely separated, and that the board of transport commissioners should be empowered to look into the situation at any time. In other words there should be no hidden subsidies from the one railway agency to the other.
Another aspect of this situation is the recommendation by the commission that there should be no discrimination in the rates charged for piggyback by the railways; that the rail freight rates for the transportation of trailers of independent trucking concerns must be equal to the rates charged for railway-owned trailers, and the equality must be enforced by law.
Turning to the question of regulation of transportation, the commission was explicit on the need for minimum rate control, minimum rate control over competitive rates of the railways under the Railway Act and minimum rate control over agreed charges under the Transport Act. Such minimum rate control 20220-9
The Address-Mr. Foy
would be enforced by the board of transport commissioners on the basis of the out of pocket costs of the railways being the lower limit for such rates.
Why did the MacPherson commission state that rate regulation of the railways must continue to stipulate a minimum limit? That stipulation is to be found at page 66 of volume II. The answer is given on the same page, as follows:
Because of their relatively enormous size and resources, and the relative permanency of investment compared to firms engaged in other modes, the railways could create intolerable uncertainty in the trucking industry by sporadic rate wars, so that an efficient trucking industry could not persist.
With all this background I find it almost impossible to believe a report carried on the front page of the Financial Times for January 13, 1964, under the heading "MacPherson report will be only partially implemented." The article was under the byline of a respected parliamentary correspondent, Mr. Warren Baldwin. It was somewhat chilling to read part of the report, which was as follows:
Railway legislation implementing parts of the MacPherson report on transportation will be ready for parliament when it reconvenes... It has lifted the hard core of the railway problem out of the report, shelving the rest temporarily or permanently.
I was even more amazed to find that the report contained a list of recommendations that were not to be implemented. How the writer acquired this knowledge I would not know. First on the list of things that have allegedly gone out the window is the amendments to the Maritime Freight Rates Act.

I judge, then, that I have permission to proceed. I should like to say this, prior to 5.45. On January 20, 1961, there was a press release issued by Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, prime minister of Canada, announcing the membership and terms of reference of the royal commission on health care. As had been previously indicated, the commission was under the chairmanship of Chief Justice Emmett Hall of Saskatchewan. I will not go into the details of the membership of the commission.
The prime minister stated that the task of the royal commission would be to make a comprehensive and independent study of the existing facilities and the future needs for health services for the people of Canada and the resources to provide such services, and to recommend such measures, consistent with the constitutional division of legislative powers in Canada, as the commissioners believe would ensure that the best possible health care was available to all Canadians.
In this connection, a number of specific areas are singled out for attention. I should like to quote from the press release:
(a)	The existing facilities and methods for providing personal health services including prevention, diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation.
(b)	Methods of improving such existing health services.
(c)	The correlation of any new or improved program with existing services with a view to providing improved health services.
(d)	The present and future requirements of personnel to provide health services.
(e)	Methods of providing adequate personnel with the best possible training and qualifications for such services.
(f)	The present physical facilities and the future requirements for the provision of adequate health services.
(g)	The estimated cost of health services now being rendered to Canadians, with projected costs of any changes that may be recommended for the extension of existing programs or for any new programs suggested.
(h)	The methods of financing health care services as presently sponsored by management, labour, professional associations, insurance companies or in any other manner.
(i)	The methods of financing any new or extended programs which may be recommended.
(j)	The relationship of existing and any recommended health care programs with medical research and the means of encouraging a high rate of scientific development in the field of medicine in Canada.
(k)	The feasibility and desirability of priorities in the development of health care services.
The commission is further empowered such other matters as it deems appropriate for the improvement of health services to all Canadians.

In view of the fact that the last couple of lines of the subamendment, which read as follows-
-a government sponsored and government operated medicare program for all Canadians.
*-are not more specific, the members of this party will support the subamendment.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING ROBBERY AT SHAWINIGAN FALLS ARMOURY

speechtext:
I would like to take this opportunity to give hon. members a report concerning the robbery which took place at Shawinigan Falls yesterday morning.
Some time before 7.45 a.m. the bandits entered the armoury at the rear security door by breaking a thick, glass plate panel in this door. When the caretaker entered at
7.45,	he was met by the armed men, bound, blindfolded and taken to the basement. Later in the morning at different times, two army personnel, a warrant officer and a captain, entered the armoury and were in turn bound, blindfolded and taken to the basement.
There were five bandits in the gang, armed with 9 mm. pistols, but no shots were fired nor were any wounds inflicted on the three victims. They wore no masks, appeared to be between the ages of 18-22 years, and seemed unfamiliar with the armoury. Before leaving at about 11.15 they wrote the letters "ALQ" on the armoury floor.
There were no other known visitors to the armoury between 7.45 a.m. and 11.45. At about
11.45,	the warrant officer freed himself and notified the police. Q.P.P., R.C.M.P. and C Pro C are investigating.
The following items were stolen:
33 FN rifles (without breech blocks),
3-	9 mm. pistols (without breech blocks),
1-C42 wireless set,
4-	No. 510 wireless sets,
7-No. 26 wireless sets,
7-field telephones,
1-Gestetner printing machine,
1-signals switchboard,
3-wireless generators,
3-wireless power units, a quantity of telephone cable, some batteries for wireless sets, magazines for the FN rifle, and military uniforms.
There was no ammunition nor explosive material in the armoury at the time of the robbery.
Damage done to the armoury consisted of many broken windows and broken door locks. The thieves damaged the filing cabinets and locks when they tried to break them open by the use of tools, when searching for the bolts and breech blocks of the stolen weapons. The gang was not successful in this attempt.
Although the caretaker stated that he saw a three-ton standard military pattern vehicle at the armoury, none of the victims heard the sound of a car when the thieves left.
As a result of the theft in Montreal, all ammunition, including ,22-inch, had been withdrawn from 62 Fd. Regt. R.C.A. Other security measures included the physical separation of bolts and breech blocks from weapons. The bolts and breech blocks were securely locked in a metal filing cabinet which thieves were unable to break into. Although the armoury is not occupied at night, all doors and windows are securely locked.
Monday, February 24, 1964
